```{r setup}
library(fivenumMeta)
has_mm <- requireNamespace("metamedian", quietly = TRUE)  # the SD case's data
has_mf <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)     # confirms the pooling
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# a number for the prose, or "(not run)" where its chunk did not run
num <- function(x, d = 1, ok = TRUE) {
  if (ok) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) else "(not run)"
}
```

```{r headline, include = FALSE}
# the two cases in brief, for the numbers of the opening paragraph; the sections
# below show the same calls one at a time
vd <- se_imputed_diff(vitd, suffixes = c(".controls", ".cases"))
hd_vd <- pool_imputed(vd)$fits
hd_vr <- matrix(NA_real_, 2, 4, dimnames = list(c("naive", "exact"),
                                                c("estimate", "se", "Q", "I2")))
if (has_mm) {
  vr <- se_imputed_diff(metamedian::dat.age, measure = "lnVR")
  hd_vr <- pool_imputed(vr)$fits
}
# the rise of the pooled standard error, in percent
up <- function(f) 100 * (f["exact", "se"] / f["naive", "se"] - 1)
```

## What the two cases show

This vignette assumes that the reader knows what `se_imputed_diff()` and `se_imputed_df()`
return: each study's imputed mean and SD with their naive and exact standard errors, in the
columns that `vignette("fivenumMeta")` describes. Start there if the columns, the scenarios or
the conventions are new.

Wu, Shi and Tong (2026) illustrate the exact standard errors on two published meta-analyses,
and this vignette runs both with the package. In a meta-analysis of means in which three of six
studies report the median and the range, the exact standard errors raise the pooled standard
error by `r num(up(hd_vd))`%. In a meta-analysis of SDs in which 29 of 51 studies
report the quartiles, they raise the pooled standard error by `r num(up(hd_vr), 0, has_mm)`%
and bring $I^2$ from `r num(hd_vr["naive", "I2"], 0, has_mm)`% to
`r num(hd_vr["exact", "I2"], 0, has_mm)`%. Both data sets are public. The vitamin D
studies ship with this package as the data set `vitd`, and the age studies come with the
`metamedian` package as its data set `dat.age`. Every number in this vignette is computed when
it is built.

Both cases pool with the common-effect model. Study $i$ gives an effect estimate $y_i$ with
variance $v_i$, and the model weights it by $w_i = 1/v_i$:
$$
\hat\theta = \frac{\sum_i w_i y_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) = \Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^{-1/2}, \qquad
\mathcal Q = \sum_i w_i (y_i - \hat\theta)^2, \qquad
I^2 = \max\Big\{0, \frac{\mathcal Q - (K - 1)}{\mathcal Q}\Big\},
$$
where $K$ is the number of studies. $\mathcal Q$ and $I^2$ are the heterogeneity measures of
Higgins and Thompson (2002).

We run each meta-analysis twice: with the naive standard errors, which treat the imputed mean
and SD as a sample mean and SD, and with the exact standard errors computed from the exact
standard deviation factors, which this package takes from the moments of the normal order
statistics of the `osmoments` package (Wu and Tong, 2026). That is, the two analyses share the
$y_i$ and differ only in the $v_i$. The function `pool_imputed()` computes the four quantities
above twice from the output of `se_imputed_diff()`, once with the naive and once with the
exact standard errors, and prints the two fits side by side. Both cases call it.

## A meta-analysis of means from medians and ranges

The data are the meta-analysis of serum vitamin D (nmol/L) in tuberculosis cases against
controls of Nnoaham and Clarke (2008), typed from their Table 1 and shipped with this package
as the data set `vitd`. Three studies report the median, minimum and maximum of each group,
two a sample mean and SD, and one a mean with the minimum and maximum.

```{r vitd}
vitd
```

The study that reports a mean with the range (Sasidharan, India) has no SD. `se_imputed_df()`
reads such a row as the scenario `mean_range`: the mean is kept as the sample mean, and the SD
is imputed from the two extremes alone, as the range divided by the expected range of a normal
sample of that size, which is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of the SD from the extremes. Its exact standard error
is the standard deviation of that estimator, from the moments of the two extremes. The
standard error of this study's mean is then $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$ under both calculations,
with the imputed SD plugged in.

The call takes the controls first, so the difference `yi` is controls minus cases, as the
paper reports it. Each group's factors are taken at its own sample size, exact at the even
sizes 40 and 38, where the reported median is the average of the two middle values under R's
default quantile definition. The table lists each study's scenario, its difference with the
two standard errors, and its weight in percent under each.

```{r vitd-diff}
d <- se_imputed_diff(vitd, suffixes = c(".controls", ".cases"))
fit_vd <- pool_imputed(d)
tab <- data.frame(study = d$study, scenario = d$scenario.cases,
                  yi = d$yi, se_naive = d$sei_naive, se_exact = d$sei,
                  w_naive = fit_vd$weights$naive,
                  w_exact = fit_vd$weights$exact)
print(tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
fit_vd
```

```{r vitd-numbers, echo = FALSE}
fits_vd <- fit_vd$fits
s1 <- d$scenario.cases == "S1"
ratio_vd <- range(d$sei[s1] / d$sei_naive[s1])
share_vd <- c(naive = sum(fit_vd$weights$naive[s1]),
              exact = sum(fit_vd$weights$exact[s1]))
# the prose below states these directions, so the build stops if the data no
# longer support them
stopifnot(ratio_vd[1] > 1, share_vd["exact"] < share_vd["naive"],
          fits_vd["exact", "se"] > fits_vd["naive", "se"])
```

Compared with the naive calculation, the exact calculation raises the standard errors of the
three studies that report the median and the range by `r num(100 * (ratio_vd[1] - 1))`% to
`r num(100 * (ratio_vd[2] - 1))`%, the inflation of the imputed mean under that
scenario at these sample sizes. Their share of the weight falls from
`r num(share_vd["naive"], 0)`% to `r num(share_vd["exact"], 0)`%. The pooled
difference moves from `r num(fits_vd["naive", "estimate"])` to
`r num(fits_vd["exact", "estimate"])` nmol/L, and its standard error from
`r num(fits_vd["naive", "se"], 2)` to `r num(fits_vd["exact", "se"], 2)`, a rise of
`r num(up(fits_vd))`%, so its confidence interval widens by the same proportion.

## A meta-analysis of SDs from quartiles

A meta-analysis of variability studies whether an outcome is more dispersed in one group than
in another. Here the effect size is the log variability ratio of Nakagawa et al. (2015), the
log of the ratio of the two groups' SDs, $y_i = \log(\hat\sigma_{i1}/\hat\sigma_{i2})$. The
data are the 51 studies of the age of COVID-19 nonsurvivors (group 1) against survivors
(group 2) of Katzenschlager et al. (2021), shipped with the `metamedian` package as its data
set `dat.age`: 29 report the three quartiles and 22 a sample mean and SD in both groups. The
question is whether age is less dispersed among those who died. `measure = "lnVR"` gives
$y_i$ with its two standard errors in place of the difference of means.

```{r age, eval = has_mm}
d <- se_imputed_diff(metamedian::dat.age, measure = "lnVR")  # suffixes .g1, .g2
table(d$scenario.g1)
fit_vr <- pool_imputed(d)
fit_vr
```

The variance of $y_i$ is approximated by the sum of one term per group, to first order in each
group's SD (the delta method, $\mathrm{Var}(\log X) \approx \mathrm{Var}(X)/(\mathrm{E}X)^2$).
The naive calculation gives every group the large-sample term of a sample SD of $n$ normal
observations, $1/\{2(n - 1)\}$. The exact calculation keeps that term for a group that gives
its sample SD and uses $C^2_\sigma(n)$, the exact variance of the imputed SD in units of
$\sigma^2$, for a group whose SD is imputed from the quartiles, which the output carries as
`(se_sigma / sigma_hat)^2`:
$$
v_i^{\mathrm{naive}} = \frac{1}{2(n_{i1} - 1)} + \frac{1}{2(n_{i2} - 1)}, \qquad
v_i^{\mathrm{exact}} = t(n_{i1}) + t(n_{i2}), \qquad
t(n) = \begin{cases}
  1/\{2(n - 1)\} & \text{for a sample SD,} \\
  C^2_\sigma(n) & \text{for an imputed SD.}
\end{cases}
$$
The columns `sei_naive` and `sei` are the square roots of these two variances. Both are
first-order approximations of the variance of a log, so the intervals below are normal
approximations. The bias correction of the log ratio of Nakagawa et al. (2015) is not applied,
as in Wu, Shi and Tong (2026). Both analyses use the plain log ratio.

```{r age-numbers, echo = FALSE, eval = has_mm}
fits_vr <- fit_vr$fits
imp <- d$scenario.g1 == "S2"
# for an imputed group, C_sigma(n)^2 over the naive term 1 / (2 (n - 1))
over <- function(se, s, n) (se / s)^2 * 2 * (n - 1)
ratio_vr <- range(c(over(d$se_sigma.g1, d$sigma_hat.g1, d$n.g1)[imp],
                    over(d$se_sigma.g2, d$sigma_hat.g2, d$n.g2)[imp]))
share_vr <- c(naive = sum(fit_vr$weights$naive[imp]),
              exact = sum(fit_vr$weights$exact[imp]))
sd_ratio <- exp(fits_vr[, "estimate"])
names(sd_ratio) <- rownames(fits_vr)
# the prose below states these directions, so the build stops if the data no
# longer support them
stopifnot(ratio_vr[1] > 1, share_vr["exact"] < share_vr["naive"],
          fits_vr["exact", "se"] > fits_vr["naive", "se"],
          fits_vr["exact", "Q"] < fits_vr["naive", "Q"],
          fits_vr["exact", "I2"] < fits_vr["naive", "I2"])
```

For a group whose SD is imputed from the quartiles, $C^2_\sigma(n)$ is
`r num(ratio_vr[1], 2, has_mm)` to `r num(ratio_vr[2], 2, has_mm)` times the naive term
$1/\{2(n - 1)\}$. Under the exact variance, the share of the weight on the 29 quartile studies
falls from `r num(share_vr["naive"], 0, has_mm)`% to `r num(share_vr["exact"], 0, has_mm)`%.
The pooled log ratio changes little, from `r num(fits_vr["naive", "estimate"], 3, has_mm)`
to `r num(fits_vr["exact", "estimate"], 3, has_mm)`, so the SD of age among nonsurvivors is
about `r num(sd_ratio["naive"], 2, has_mm)` times that among survivors either way. Its
standard error, however, rises by `r num(up(fits_vr), 0, has_mm)`%, from
`r num(fits_vr["naive", "se"], 4, has_mm)` to `r num(fits_vr["exact", "se"], 4, has_mm)`, and
its confidence interval widens by the same proportion. $\mathcal Q$ falls from
`r num(fits_vr["naive", "Q"], 1, has_mm)` to `r num(fits_vr["exact", "Q"], 1, has_mm)`, and
$I^2$ from `r num(fits_vr["naive", "I2"], 0, has_mm)`% to `r num(fits_vr["exact", "I2"], 0, has_mm)`%.
Since the two fits share the $y_i$ and differ only in the variances, the fall in
$\mathcal Q$ and $I^2$ comes from the larger within-study variances alone: the extra spread of
an imputed SD, which the naive variance leaves out, was counted as heterogeneity.

With the `metafor` package, the exact fit is `rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d, method = "EE")`,
which returns the same pooled estimate, standard error and $\mathcal Q$, and the naive fit
takes `sei_naive` in the same way:

```{r metafor, eval = has_mm && has_mf}
f <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d, method = "EE")
c(estimate = as.numeric(f$b), se = f$se, Q = f$QE, I2 = f$I2)
```

```{r not-run, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# printed only when metamedian was missing at build time, so the numbers of
# this case read "(not run)"
if (!has_mm) cat("The package metamedian was not available when this",
                 "vignette was built, so the SD case did not run. Install it",
                 "and rebuild the vignette, or run the calls above in a",
                 "session that has it.\n")
```

```{r check, include = FALSE}
# the sections above and the headline chunk agree, and so does metafor
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fits_vd, hd_vd)))
if (has_mm) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fits_vr, hd_vr)))
if (has_mm && has_mf) {
  ours <- unlist(fits_vr["exact", c("estimate", "se", "Q")], use.names = FALSE)
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c(as.numeric(f$b), f$se, f$QE), ours)))
}
```

## References

Higgins JPT, Thompson SG (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in
Medicine 21(11), 1539-1558.

Katzenschlager S, Zimmer AJ, Gottschalk C, Grafeneder J, Schmitz S, Kraker S, Ganslmeier M,
Muth A, Seitel A, Maier-Hein L, Benedetti A, Larmann J, Weigand MA, McGrath S, Denkinger CM
(2021). Can we predict the severe course of
COVID-19, a systematic review and meta-analysis of indicators of clinical outcome? PLOS One
16, e0255154.

McGrath S, Zhao X, Ozturk O, Katzenschlager S, Steele R, Benedetti A (2024). metamedian: An R
package for meta-analyzing studies reporting medians. Research Synthesis Methods 15(2),
332-346.

Nakagawa S, Poulin R, Mengersen K, Reinhold K, Engqvist L, Lagisz M, Senior AM (2015).
Meta-analysis of variation: ecological and evolutionary applications and beyond. Methods in
Ecology and Evolution 6(2), 143-152.

Nnoaham KE, Clarke A (2008). Low serum vitamin D levels and tuberculosis: a systematic review
and meta-analysis. International Journal of Epidemiology 37(1), 113-119.

Viechtbauer W (2010). Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of
Statistical Software 36(3), 1-48.

Wu Z, Shi J, Tong T (2026). Precision of the imputed mean and standard deviation from a
five-number summary. Manuscript.

R. Manuscript.
